question: Which prospects seem most likely to purchase, based on the conversations?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every explicit buying signal or obstacle in this prospect call: stated budget or budget approval status, decision-making authority of attendees, purchase timeline or deadline, named next steps (pilot, trial, proposal, contract, security review), requested pricing or quotes, objections or blockers raised, competing vendors being considered, and any direct statement of intent or hesitation by the prospect, quoting the speaker where possible. Also note the call's stage (discovery, evaluation, technical review) and whether the prospect ended the call with a committed follow-up.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as the Prospect call type (CALL-001 to CALL-010), since these are new-business calls.
Likelihood to purchase is a judgement drawn from the conversation content, so the reader must extract evidence rather than give a score, allowing comparison across calls.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows
findings.context: Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations) states she is interested enough to test OrbitFlow and will supply three real workflows if given a sandbox. — Named next step: sandbox pilot, conditional on exception handling holding up. Stated intent to test, not to buy.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria. Then we decide on the sandbox.
findings.context: Agreed next steps: OrbitFlow sends security pack and architecture summary; customer sends representative workflow and sample data; jointly write three to five pilot success criteria, then decide on sandbox. — Named next steps before any sandbox is granted.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: That's the intent. It'll slip. It always slips. But that's the plan.
findings.context: Target timeline is vendor selection before end of July with first workflows live in September, but Rachel expects it to slip. — Purchase timeline; customer self-qualifies it as optimistic.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's more than I expected.
findings.context: Pricing reaction: Growth starts at $1,800/month (up to 30 users, annual) and Rachel says it is more than expected, benchmarked against Zapier; she needs a clearer ROI story to justify it. — Price objection raised; Enterprise is custom-priced. Maya deferred a firm number until the user model is known.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
findings.context: Main commercial obstacle: the real decision is whether to expand the existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor; Rachel says she must win that internally. — Competing alternative and internal blocker; Tom also frames the honest comparison as Workato or improving current tooling.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
findings.context: Tom Alvarez frames the honest comparison as Workato or improving the existing setup, not doing nothing. — Competing vendor/status quo; Maya agreed to define the pilot against it.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I own the project. IT security and the VP of Customer Success sign off. Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year
findings.context: Decision process: Rachel owns the project; IT security and VP Customer Success sign off; finance is involved above $25k per year. — Decision-maker authority and approval thresholds. Rachel is VP RevOps; budget authority beyond her is implied, not confirmed.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: One representative workflow working with real enough data. Security gates understood. A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Stated conditions to move to decision: one representative workflow working with real data, security gates understood, a commercial model without scaling surprises, and operators believing they can own it. — Explicit decision criteria; hesitation about operating ownership.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The gating issue isn't security for us.
findings.context: Security is not a gate for the customer; Tom expects a standard review and does not require data residency. Customer asked for documentation, not just questionnaire answers. — Security review as a step, not a blocker.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit.
findings.context: Tom Alvarez flags that a demo that looks great could become another tool the team must babysit; concern about ownership and maintainability. — Hesitation on operating burden, not on price.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction.
findings.context: Rachel explicitly rejects an ROI case based on headcount reduction; value must come from consistency and speed. — Internal sell-case constraint affecting budget justification.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Great. Send it over and we'll come back with sample inputs.
findings.context: Call stage is discovery/first demo; no committed follow-up beyond agreeing to a written recap, security pack, and joint pilot criteria. Customer ended positively but conditionally. — Call stage and closing commitment. Overall tone is interested but conditional (inferred).

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
findings.context: Prospect is in technical discovery; the BAA is a hard gate. Elliot Greene says OrbitFlow cannot be used for any workflow that may involve PHI without a BAA. — Security/compliance blocker raised by the security architect, who has veto power over the deal.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer's no, the price is irrelevant.
findings.context: Priya Shah states procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security answers the BAA question, so price is irrelevant if the answer is no. — Pricing was presented (Growth from $1,800/month, Enterprise custom) but the prospect deferred it, signalling pricing is not an active buying step yet.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I'm the sponsor — business systems. Security can veto, as you've seen. Privacy counsel reviews the DPA and the BAA. Procurement handles final terms.
findings.context: Priya Shah is the sponsor, but the decision needs multiple approvers: security can veto, privacy counsel reviews DPA and BAA, procurement handles final terms. — Decision-making authority; the sponsor has budget-owner-like standing but is not the sole decision maker.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm. But we could run a non-sensitive proof of concept in August — synthetic data, or clearly non-PHI.
findings.context: Prospect states no production launch before Q4, but a non-sensitive proof of concept could run in August using synthetic or non-PHI data. — Purchase timeline and proposed pilot; the timeline is constrained by the regulatory gate.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: My read is I would still consider a limited pilot with synthetic or clearly non-PHI data. But I want to be explicit about something: a successful pilot would not automatically mean we can deploy broadly.
findings.context: Priya Shah would still consider a limited pilot, but a successful pilot would not automatically mean broad deployment; these are two decisions with different approvers. — Conditional interest in a pilot, with explicit hesitation about broad rollout.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Separately, and this is the one that matters, a written position on the BAA within a week. You send us the representative workflow and some sample data, ideally messy. And we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
findings.context: Named next steps: OrbitFlow sends the security pack and a written BAA position within a week; prospect sends a representative workflow with sample data; both sides jointly write three to five pilot success criteria; a permission-model session for Elliot is scheduled. — Committed follow-up on both sides, with the BAA written answer as the critical item.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have. Those are the real competitors, not another workflow vendor.
findings.context: Competing alternatives named by the prospect: Power Automate (already covered by the Microsoft agreement) or improving existing processes. Priya calls these the real competitors, not another workflow vendor. — Competing options; Power Automate licensing is a procurement-relevant factor.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: One representative workflow working with real enough data. The security gates understood, and by understood I mean answered. A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises. And the people who'd operate it believing they can own it.
findings.context: Prospect has explicit conditions for a decision: one representative workflow working with real enough data, security gates answered, a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises, and operators believing they can own it. — Decision criteria stated at end of call; the prospect is in technical discovery, not yet evaluation or commit.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I'd say eleven weeks for anything non-trivial. It was six in January.
findings.context: Pain driving interest: a growing backlog of eleven weeks for non-trivial automation requests, up from six in January; the prospect values the systems-group time saved as the pilot baseline. — Stated business case for buying; the prospect said ROI would not be framed as headcount.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Honestly? I'm not ready to react to that.
findings.context: Prospect declined to react to Enterprise pricing on this call and asked for a per-user model before any figure is quoted; no budget or budget approval status was stated. — Budget not discussed; pricing deferred pending user model and security outcome.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: The blocker is regulatory, not technical, and until it's answered nothing else moves.
findings.context: Overall the prospect appears cautiously interested but gated: the BAA blocker must be resolved before anything else moves, and the vendor itself said so. — Inferred from the vendor summary and the prospect's conditional statements; the prospect did not state a purchase intent.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
findings.context: Prospect states budget gap: $1,800/month Growth price is hard for team size; she had $800-1,000 in mind. — Stated budget obstacle during pricing discussion; vendor acknowledged the gap.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I can choose tools under fifteen thousand a year on my own. Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
findings.context: Decision authority is limited: Sophie can approve tools under $15,000/year alone; above that it goes to COO and finance director, a slower process. — Stated approval path; the $21,600 annual price exceeds her threshold.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Twenty-one, six. So it goes upstairs. Which is a different conversation and a slower one.
findings.context: Sophie's price is above her own approval threshold; the deal would go upstairs to a slower process. — Sophie computes $1,800/month as $21,600/year and says it goes upstairs.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Ideally something in place by early October, because after that nobody's changing anything until January.
findings.context: Target timeline: have something in place by early October, with a decision around August if they proceed. — Holiday freeze (no changes in November) constrains the timeline; vendor proposed August decision.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Honestly? Zapier and Make.
findings.context: Named competing alternatives are Zapier (keep) and Make; prospect has tested Make. — Prospect describes the real alternative to OrbitFlow; ownership and maintenance are concerns with both.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
findings.context: Prospect names budget as the biggest risk and says keeping Zapier is a real possible outcome. — Stated objection; prospect explicitly open to not buying.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Prospect is not convinced value closes the price gap versus tools already paid for, though she likes monitoring and reusable templates. — Stated hesitation at end of call; she also says she is not saying no.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
findings.context: Prospect asked whether annual prepay would materially reduce price; vendor said it is a meaningful discount but not a halving. — Requested pricing lever; vendor did not commit to a specific discount.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Then yes. Send me that.
findings.context: Prospect committed to a follow-up: Marcus will log time on broken automations for four weeks; Sophie agreed to send three worst automations. — Committed next steps at end of call, with vendor owing written answers on Shopify trigger coverage and EU processing region.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'd rather have a considered maybe than an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement.
findings.context: Call stage is discovery/demo; no purchase commitment or formal evaluation step beyond the agreed logging exercise and written follow-ups. — Vendor framed it as an early, considered maybe rather than a yes.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Enterprise applications sponsors, which is me. Then the architecture board, information security, the works council for some workflow monitoring use cases, procurement, and regional IT.
findings.context: Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications) is the enterprise applications sponsor and the decision process involves six groups: architecture board, information security, works council, procurement, regional IT, and his own sponsorship. — Decision-making authority and buying process; Martin names the groups, and notes which can say no.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Architecture board and information security. Regional IT cannot say no formally but can make implementation impossible, which amounts to the same thing.
findings.context: Architecture board and information security can formally say no; regional IT cannot formally say no but can make implementation impossible. — Veto authority within the buying process.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Formal architecture review in September. Procurement in Q4. Realistic production use early next year.
findings.context: Procurement is the last step and will take as long as it takes; formal architecture review in September, procurement in Q4, realistic production use early next year. — Purchase timeline stated by the prospect.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Regional IT will have opinions. That is not a formal gate but it is a real one. And procurement has a standard process that takes as long as it takes.
findings.context: Anika Bose says procurement's standard process takes as long as it takes, and regional IT is a real gate. — Procurement and regional IT obstacle raised during governance discussion.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
findings.context: The biggest blocker is whether SAP and on-premise systems make implementation too heavy for the first use case; if it needs nine months of integration work, they would choose a different use case or not proceed. — Stated decision criterion and key obstacle.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: MuleSoft and custom integration services. We already own MuleSoft.
findings.context: Prospect considers MuleSoft plus custom integration services a real alternative to OrbitFlow, a competing path that could be proposed internally. — Competing option, though Martin does not think it is a good idea.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: So — send us the architecture material first.
findings.context: Next step is architecture material first, not a sandbox; sandbox and pilot only if deployment model is viable. Vendor committed to deliver architecture note and security pack; customer committed to SAP operations list, promotion process documentation, and an hour with SAP interface owners by end of next week. — Committed follow-up ending the call.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Good. Send all of it. We will also send our questionnaire. It is two hundred and forty questions.
findings.context: Anika Bose says the Enterprise security and governance requirements are a precondition; she has a 240-question questionnaire and will send it. — Governance gate; prospect is engaged but conditional.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Three months is optimistic. Six is realistic if the use case is contested.
findings.context: Works council co-determination could take six months if the use case is contested, a timeline risk for workflows monitoring employees. — Obstacle raised by the governance lead.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I see strategic potential here. But I do not think a sandbox is the next step.
findings.context: Martin states he sees strategic potential but does not think a sandbox is the next step; he is hesitant about committing before deployment viability is proven. — Direct statement of intent and hesitation about next step.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review.
findings.context: Enterprise licence pricing is expected; customer wants transparency on services and premium connectors, and wants the user model explicit, with no surprise full-seat costs for occasional approvers. — Pricing expectations; no quote requested yet, vendor committed to separated line items.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I could ask. I would rather give you a real one later than an invented one now.
findings.context: Stage is enterprise discovery; no budget figure or formal approval status was stated, and the prospect declined to give a number on the cost of data mismatches. — Budget signal is absent; ROI figures are estimates.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: You and Tray.io. We've had a Tray proof of concept running for about six weeks. This isn't a discovery call for us
findings.context: Prospect is running a formal bake-off against Tray.io with a six-week Tray proof of concept already underway; this is an evaluation, not discovery. — Stage and competitive landscape stated at call open by the prospect's executive sponsor.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: I'm the executive sponsor and I'm broadly positive. Hannah and platform engineering score technical fit. Then security, legal, procurement, and the COO approve.
findings.context: Executive sponsor is broadly positive, but approval requires technical fit scoring plus security, legal, procurement, and COO sign-off, so many gates could kill the deal. — Decision-making authority and approval chain for the purchase.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
findings.context: Senior Risk Engineer Hannah Cole names model-risk and auditability as the gates that could kill the project; she is the most likely blocker. — Objection/blocker raised by a non-signing technical approver.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
findings.context: Model-risk governance is a potential blocker: AI in a decision path would trigger a nine-month process. — Objection tied to internal model risk framework; partially resolved by vendor saying AI steps are optional and explicit.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint.
findings.context: Vendor could not confirm that AI outputs are enforced as leaf nodes; it is a convention, not a platform control, and is recorded as a known limitation. — Real gap acknowledged by vendor; customer asked it be written down.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Then that's satisfactory, subject to seeing the actual payload schema.
findings.context: Customer accepts the exportable audit history requirement as satisfactory, subject to seeing the actual payload schema, which vendor agreed to send. — Audit gate partially cleared at technical level.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Assuming the security material lines up, I want to move. Send sandbox access and a written proposal for a six-week pilot
findings.context: Prospect is moving toward a six-week pilot against Tray if security material lines up, with sandbox and written proposal requested. — Committed next step at call end, conditional on security pack.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Vendor decision in August. First controlled production workflows in October.
findings.context: Timeline: technical bake-off July, vendor decision August, first controlled production workflows October, driven by a remediation programme with a fixed date. — Purchase timeline and deadline.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It has a remediation programme, which has a budget, which is a number. Yes.
findings.context: The remediation programme deadline is the timeline driver, tied to an audit finding with a budget. — Budget/urgency signal; the audit finding has a remediation budget but no figure given.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it
findings.context: Enterprise pricing is custom; Growth tier is 1800 a month up to 30 users annually. Prospect expects Enterprise range and is concerned about usage overages in year two. — Requested pricing and cost objection.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: You'll have them Friday.
findings.context: Vendor will model volumes at 300 and 500 users before quoting; prospect requested itemised seat split and a cap, and volume estimates were promised by Friday. — Pricing next step; vendor declined to promise a cap before modelling.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's also "keep the scripts and document them better." That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
findings.context: Main competitive threat is not only Tray but a cheaper internal option of keeping scripts and documenting them; prospect believes it would be proposed and could cost two months. — Alternative/competing option raised by prospect.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
findings.context: Prospect states the deciding factors versus Tray are debugging experience and programmatic audit export; connector breadth is a tie. — Stated decision criteria.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It's not a two-horse bake-off, it's a two-horse bake-off where one horse has a six-week head start.
findings.context: Hannah Cole corrects the framing: it is a two-horse bake-off where one horse has a six-week head start. — Self-correction of competitive position by prospect.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Not currently.
findings.context: Possible integration blocker: internal Kafka-based event bus is not reachable from outside the network; vendor wants an hour with its owner. — Technical obstacle; not a decision blocker stated yet.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: I'll need a week.
findings.context: Prospect ended the call with committed follow-ups on both sides: vendor to send security pack, schema, sandbox, and proposal; prospect to deliver volume estimates Friday and sign off a week for security review. — Committed follow-up at close.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: We say eighty.
findings.context: Overall likelihood of purchase appears moderate-to-positive but conditional: strong pain and fixed deadline, yet gated on security, model-risk, and pricing outcomes. — Inferred from the full call; no explicit budget approval or signed commitment.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
findings.context: Prospect's signing authority is capped at £20k; contracts above that need founder approval, which is a hard limit. — Budget/authority obstacle raised by COO when pricing of £21.5k/year was discussed.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: It's a hard limit. And more to the point, if I have to take it to him, he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
findings.context: Imogen says the price is a hard limit and the founder would need a better justification than robustness versus Zapier. — Price objection; the founder will ask what the extra £21k buys over ~£2k Zapier.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: So our Growth package is eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement.
findings.context: Growth package priced at £1,800/month on annual agreement for up to 30 users; prospect said this is above her budget. — Vendor's stated pricing; prospect reacted negatively.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
findings.context: Prospect explicitly said the price is above what she had in mind. — Budget objection right after pricing.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Is there any way to start with ten users? Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
findings.context: Prospect asked for a smaller start (10 users) or monthly billing to pilot before an annual commitment; vendor said monthly was 'usually fine' but needed manager approval, and the prospect asked for confirmation. — Requested alternative pricing; vendor not confirmed; committed to check and come back.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: The thirty is the package, so the price is the price.
findings.context: Vendor refused to reduce the 30-user package; prospect objected to paying for unneeded seats. — Seat count objection; vendor says price is fixed to the package.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough for a company that doesn't have an IT team. That's a real possibility
findings.context: Prospect is considering staying with Zapier plus better process discipline as an alternative, a real possibility. — Competing option / possible no-decision; prospect said they would be doing their job badly not to consider it.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So — I'm interested. I'm not dismissing it.
findings.context: Prospect expressed interest but not dismissal, and wants a recorded, use-case-specific demo to share with the founder and ops manager by end of week. — Stage is discovery moving toward evaluation; committed follow-up is a vendor deliverable, not a signed next step.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We've got a new client-services process launching in September.
findings.context: Prospect's timeline: needs something running before a new client-services process launches in September; otherwise they will be stuck with old tooling for another year. — Purchase timing driver; vendor said September is no problem.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Can we see that in writing?
findings.context: Prospect wants a reference from an agency customer and written DPA/no-training assurance before proceeding; vendor committed to send both. — Due diligence and security requirements; these are pending vendor actions.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
findings.context: Prospect is checking whether SSO is included on all plans, doubting vendor's claim; vendor said 'fairly sure' and would confirm. — Open item affecting package fit; a competing vendor treated SSO as enterprise-only.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
findings.context: Decision authority: Imogen is COO and cannot sign above £20k without founder; Ben (Head of Client Services) raised objections and requirements; the founder and ops manager are the audience for the demo. — Attendee decision-making authority; neither attendee is the final approver for this price.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: A reference in an agency would be useful, if you've got one.
findings.context: Vendor's sales-rep reasoning rested on ROI and a 'lost client' story; the prospect treated the case as unproven and asked for an agency reference. — Vendor pitch versus prospect skepticism; the reference was not confirmed.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Well. Let's see.
findings.context: Call ended with the prospect not committed; the prospect said 'Let's see' and vendor's follow-ups (demo, DPA, reference, SSO and monthly-billing confirmations) are pending. — No committed purchase; follow-ups are vendor-owned.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: So I'm exploring alternatives. That's what this is. I want to be honest that it's exploration, not a procurement process.
findings.context: Prospect states the deal is exploratory, not a procurement process, and realistically no decision this year. — Explicit low purchase intent/timeline; budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so any action would be in that cycle.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so if anything were to happen it'd be in that cycle.
findings.context: Budget timing: any possible purchase would fall in the next fiscal year budgeting cycle starting October. — Timeline obstacle; no current-year budget.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
findings.context: Power Automate is already embedded, licensed and approved, creating a strong competing/incumbent obstacle; OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify switching. — Competing solution and key blocker; first-class Dynamics gap acknowledged by vendor.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: What I'm not going to tell you is that we have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector on the market
findings.context: Vendor admits OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, which the prospect treats as the biggest issue. — Vendor objection-surfacing; Dynamics 365 is mandatory.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
findings.context: Microsoft platform team is expected to strongly oppose the decision and has killed things before; formally influence, not veto. — Decision-making influence and blocker; decision authority of attendees is limited.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
findings.context: Prospect's licensing concern: several hundred supervisors would need approval/view access and must not require full seats; otherwise the deal is over. — Pricing/per-seat objection; approver population vs builder seats.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
findings.context: Prospect said the price might be defensible for central operations but the licensing model is what matters; no quote requested and vendor deliberately withheld a number. — Pricing discussion; growth tier quoted at 1800/month up to 30 users, no proposal requested.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: I'd rather have a roadmap and architecture conversation than a commercial proposal at this point.
findings.context: Prospect explicitly wants a roadmap and architecture conversation, not a commercial proposal, as the next step; committed follow-up is the architecture session plus internal measurement of debugging time. — Named next step; no proposal or pilot committed yet.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: I'm curious, but this is still early.
findings.context: Prospect is curious and sees value in a possible future purchase if the Dynamics integration direction and offline patterns look right; the business case rests on operational cost of troubleshooting. — Positive interest conditioned on two technical proofs; cost argument must be made internally.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: It was a guess.
findings.context: Prospect would need to measure team time spent debugging flows before making the internal cost argument; the day-a-week figure was an unverified guess. — Business case gap; estimate not confirmed.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Do the same test in Power Automate at the same time. If it's not better, you should know.
